title: wait, notify and guarded blocks
goal: By the end you can write a guarded block with `wait()` in a `while` loop, choose between `notify()` and `notifyAll()`, and build a bounded buffer from scratch.

warmup.q: Two consumers wait on an empty queue with `if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return queue.removeFirst();`. A producer adds one item and calls `notifyAll()`. What happens?
options: One consumer gets the item and the other keeps waiting
Both wake; one gets the item and the other throws NoSuchElementException
notifyAll() wakes only one of them, so nothing goes wrong
Both get the same item
warmup.why: `notifyAll()` wakes both. They get the lock back one at a time. The first takes the item. The second is already past its `if`, so it calls `removeFirst()` on an empty queue. With `while` instead of `if`, the second would check again and go back to waiting.

sections.h: Always wait in a while loop, never an if
sections.body:
When `wait()` returns, the condition you waited for may not hold. There are two reasons.

The first is in the Javadoc for `Object.wait`: "A thread can wake up without being notified, interrupted, or timing out, a so-called spurious wakeup." It is rare. It is also allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting if it is not met.

The second reason happens all the time. `notifyAll()` wakes every waiter, but they take the lock back one at a time, and other threads may get in first. Two consumers wait on an empty queue. A producer adds one item and calls `notifyAll()`. Consumer 1 gets the lock first and takes the item. Consumer 2 gets the lock next, and the queue is empty again. If consumer 2 checked with `if`, it is already past its check:

```java
if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait();   // checked once, before waiting
return queue.removeFirst();         // NoSuchElementException
```

```kotlin
if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait()    // checked once, before waiting
return queue.removeFirst()          // NoSuchElementException
```

With `while`, consumer 2 checks again, sees the empty queue and goes back to waiting. That is all a guarded block is: a `while` loop around `wait()`, with the condition as the loop test.

The habit costs nothing, so make it unconditional. Every `wait()` sits inside `while (!condition)`. In a code review, treat an `if` around `wait()` as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It has just never had two waiters at the same time yet.

sections.h: Prefer notifyAll, because notify wakes one thread, maybe the wrong one
sections.body:
`notify()` wakes one thread from the wait set, and you don't get to choose which. That is fine when every waiter waits for the same condition and any one of them can use the change. It breaks when one monitor has waiters for different conditions.

A bounded buffer is the classic case. Producers wait for "not full", consumers wait for "not empty", and with a plain monitor they share one wait set. Picture a buffer with one slot, two producers and two consumers, all using `notify()`:

1. The slot is empty, so both consumers wait.
2. Producer 1 fills the slot and wakes consumer 1. Before consumer 1 gets the lock, both producers find the slot full and wait. The wait set now holds producer 1, producer 2 and consumer 2.
3. Consumer 1 empties the slot and calls `notify()`, which happens to wake consumer 2, the wrong kind.
4. Consumer 2 finds the slot empty and waits again. Consumer 1 loops, finds it empty too, and waits.

Now all four threads wait for a signal nobody will send. No thread holds the lock, so it isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense, but the program has stopped just the same. The demo below gets there within a handful of items.

So the default is `notifyAll()`. It wakes every waiter, each one re-checks its own condition in its `while` loop, and the ones that can't go on wait again. The price is extra wake-ups when many threads wait, which rarely matters next to a stalled pipeline.

Use `notify()` only when both of these hold: every waiter waits for the same condition, and one change lets at most one of them proceed. If you need precise wake-ups for two kinds of waiters, give each kind its own `Condition` on a `ReentrantLock`. That is lesson 7 of this track.

figure.caption: wait() moves the owner to the wait set and gives the lock back. notify moves a waiter back to the entry set, where it must win the lock again, so it must re-check its condition.

analogy: A monitor is a meeting room with one key. People who want the room queue in the corridor (the entry set, BLOCKED). The one inside can decide they can't continue yet, hang the key back up and go to the lounge next door (the wait set, WAITING). When someone in the room changes things, they can call into the lounge: `notify()` sends one person back to the corridor, `notifyAll()` sends everyone. Nobody walks from the lounge straight into the room. They queue for the key again, and by the time they get in, the thing they waited for may be gone, which is why they must look again. The analogy breaks at spurious wakeups: people don't leave the lounge for no reason, but a Java thread is allowed to.
in_your_world: You'll rarely hand-write `wait()` in a payments service, and when you do it should look like the buffer above. You meet guarded blocks all the time inside libraries. A connection pool with 20 connections makes the 21st request wait until a connection is returned. A `KafkaProducer` blocks `send()` for up to `max.block.ms` when its buffer memory is full. A Quarkus worker pool queues requests when every worker is busy. In a thread dump those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Reading the stack tells you which condition they wait for, and that usually tells you which resource ran out.
mistake: The most common real mistake is using `wait()` and `notify()` as a bare signal, with no condition to check: one thread calls `lock.wait()` "until the result is ready", another calls `lock.notify()` when it is. If the notify happens before the waiter starts waiting, the signal is lost and the waiter sleeps forever. This is a lost wake-up. It passes tests because the waiter usually gets there first. The fix is to always wait for a state, never for an event: set a field such as `ready = true` under the lock before notifying, and wait with `while (!ready) lock.wait();`. A notify that came early is then harmless, because the waiter sees `ready` and never waits.

compare.title: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BoundedBuffer.java

kotlin.title: KotlinGuarded.kt

compare.note: Kotlin's `Any` does not expose `wait()`, `notify()` or `notifyAll()`. The Kotlin samples in this lesson get them by using a `java.lang.Object` as the lock, which works but earns a compiler warning that you have to suppress. The idiomatic replacement is a `ReentrantLock` with a `Condition`: `withLock { }` takes and releases the lock, `await()` plays the part of `wait()`, and `signalAll()` the part of `notifyAll()`. The rules don't change. `Condition` allows spurious wakeups too, so you still wait in a `while` loop. As a bonus, one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers can wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds on exactly that.

worked.title: Wait for a settlement file, with a deadline

steps.say: A batch job must wait until the settlement file has arrived, but give up after 30 seconds. Here is the first attempt. What can go wrong?

It is the `if` bug in a new shape. A spurious wakeup, or a `notifyAll()` meant for some other condition on the same lock, returns early with `fileArrived` still false, after 2 seconds instead of 30. Simply putting `wait(30_000)` in a `while` loop is wrong too: every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The fix is to compute a deadline once and wait for what is left of it.
The guard loop now checks the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the remaining time.

The side that receives the file sets the state before it signals, both under the lock. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter sees `fileArrived` and never calls `wait()`. Why does the waiter use `System.nanoTime()` and not `System.currentTimeMillis()`?
`nanoTime()` only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. `currentTimeMillis()` is wall-clock time, and NTP can move it backwards or forwards, which would stretch or cut the timeout.

lab.title: Build a bounded buffer with wait and notifyAll
steps: Run the tests. All six fail, some only after a few seconds, because the threads that should wait die instead.
Add the fields: a private lock object, an `ArrayDeque` for the items, the capacity. Reject a capacity below 1 in the constructor.
Write `put`: guard with `while (full) lock.wait();`, add at the tail, `notifyAll()`.
Write `take`: guard with `while (empty) lock.wait();`, remove the head, `notifyAll()`, return it. Write `size()` under the lock.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. The 4-producer, 4-consumer test is the one that catches `if` and `notify()` mistakes.
hints: The blocking tests poll `getState()` until it says WAITING. A thread that sleeps in a loop shows TIMED_WAITING and fails them. Use `wait()` with no timeout.
Call `wait()` and `notifyAll()` on the same object you synchronize on. Calling `wait()` on `this` while holding `lock` throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
Don't catch `InterruptedException` inside the buffer. Let it propagate: both methods already declare it.
lab.done_when: All six tests in `BoundedBufferTest` pass, three runs in a row.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A guarded block holds the lock, checks a condition, and calls `wait()` until it holds. `wait()` releases the monitor while it waits and retakes it before returning.
You must hold an object's monitor to call its `wait()`, `notify()` or `notifyAll()`, or you get `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
Always `while (!condition) wait();`. Spurious wakeups are allowed, and another thread may change the state before you get the lock back.
`notify()` wakes one arbitrary waiter. With two kinds of waiters on one monitor it can wake the wrong kind and stall everything. Default to `notifyAll()`.
Wait for a state, not an event: set a field before notifying, so an early signal is never lost.

options: Nothing, since nobody is waiting
It wakes every thread in the JVM that is waiting on any lock
It throws IllegalMonitorStateException, because the thread doesn't hold lock's monitor
It blocks until some thread waits on lock
quiz.why: `wait`, `notify` and `notifyAll` require the caller to own the object's monitor, so they must run inside `synchronized (lock)`. It doesn't matter that nobody is waiting. The check comes first.

quiz.q: A thread wakes up from `lock.wait()` because another thread called `notifyAll()`. When does it run the line after `wait()`?
options: Immediately, in parallel with the notifier
After it gets the monitor back, which is at the earliest when the notifier leaves its synchronized block
Only after every other woken thread has finished
Never: it has to call wait() again
quiz.why: `notifyAll()` doesn't release the lock. The woken threads move back to competing for the monitor, and `wait()` returns only once this thread owns it again. Other woken threads may get it first and change the state, which is why the condition must be re-checked.

quiz.q: A one-slot buffer has 2 producers and 2 consumers, and both `put` and `take` call `notify()`. Each `wait()` is correctly inside a `while`. What can happen?
options: Nothing bad, because the while loops make it safe
Two consumers take the same item
IllegalMonitorStateException
All four threads end up waiting with nobody left to notify them
quiz.why: The `while` loops protect against acting on a false condition, not against lost signals. If a consumer's `notify()` wakes the other consumer instead of a producer, that wake-up is wasted, and soon every thread waits. `notifyAll()`, or one `Condition` per kind of waiter, fixes it.

quiz.q: A worker calls `lock.wait()` with no condition, "until the report is done". The reporting thread calls `lock.notifyAll()` when it finishes. Sometimes the worker waits forever. Why?
options: notifyAll() only wakes threads that started waiting before it was called, so an early report is a lost wake-up
wait() without a timeout is not allowed
notifyAll() needs a second call to wake a thread
The worker must call notify() itself
quiz.why: A notification wakes only threads that are already waiting. If the report finishes first, the signal goes nowhere, and the worker then waits for a signal that already happened. Wait for a state: `while (!done) lock.wait();`, with `done = true` set before `notifyAll()`.

quiz.q: From A thread's life: a consumer is parked inside `lock.wait()` and another thread interrupts it. Which is true?
options: wait() returns normally and the interrupt flag stays set
wait() throws InterruptedException at once, without retaking the monitor
Nothing happens until someone calls notify()
wait() retakes the monitor, then throws InterruptedException with the interrupt flag cleared
quiz.why: Like `sleep`, `wait` reacts to an interrupt by throwing `InterruptedException` and clearing the flag. It retakes the monitor first, so your catch or finally block still runs inside the synchronized block. Restore the flag or let the exception propagate.

flashcards.back: It releases lock's monitor, parks the thread in the wait set (WAITING), and retakes the monitor before it returns.
Spurious wakeups are allowed, and another thread may change the state between the notify and the moment you get the lock back.

flashcards.front: What happens if you call `wait()` or `notify()` without holding that object's monitor?

flashcards.back: No. The woken threads compete for the monitor after the notifier leaves its synchronized block.

flashcards.front: When is `notify()` safe to use instead of `notifyAll()`?
flashcards.back: Only when every waiter waits for the same condition and each change lets at most one waiter proceed.
A notify that happens before anyone waits. If the waiter has no condition to check, it then waits forever. Fix: wait for a state field, set before notifying.

terms.plain: Code that waits, under a lock, until a condition holds: `while (!cond) lock.wait();`.
The threads parked in `wait()` on one monitor, waiting to be notified.
A return from `wait()` with no notify, interrupt or timeout. Allowed by the spec.
Wake every thread in the monitor's wait set. They then compete for the lock.
A signal sent before anyone waits for it, so the waiter never hears it.
Making a fast producer wait when the consumer can't keep up, instead of buffering without limit.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a bounded buffer built on one monitor needs `while` loops and `notifyAll()`, and what goes wrong if you use `if` or `notify()` instead.
explain_back.answer: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty", but with one monitor they share one wait set. When a thread wakes, the state may already have changed again, because other woken threads can get the lock first, and spurious wakeups are allowed. So each waiter must re-check its condition in a `while` loop; with `if`, a consumer can wake up and remove from an empty buffer. `notify()` wakes one arbitrary waiter, which may be the wrong kind: a consumer waking another consumer wastes the only signal, and eventually every thread waits with nobody to wake them. `notifyAll()` wakes everyone, and the loops send the ones that can't proceed back to waiting.

deeper.body:
Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. `wait(millis)` returns when notified, interrupted, spuriously, or when the time is up, and it does not tell you which. That is why the worked example tracks its own deadline with `System.nanoTime()`.

The JVM has bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That is a good reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write.

Two observability notes. JFR has a `jdk.JavaMonitorWait` event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a `jdk.JavaMonitorNotify` event. And on virtual threads, `Object.wait()` used to pin the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases.

Finally, the history. `wait`/`notify` have been in Java since 1.0. `java.util.concurrent` arrived in Java 5 with `Condition`, `BlockingQueue` and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called `AbstractQueuedSynchronizer`. When you read the source of `ArrayBlockingQueue`, you'll find the same guard, act and signal parts as in this lesson, written with a `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s.
